title: Not more books
hook: progress isn't reading more, it's how you desire and avoid (Discourses 1.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: kin to the divine, and your line, kin. Did you catch yourself shrinking, and stand up a little straighter? Day three hundred ninety-four.

There's a stack of books by your bed, or a list of podcasts, or forty saved articles about becoming calmer. Finishing them can look like progress. A student in Epictetus' classroom felt the same way. He walked up holding a scroll by Chrysippus, the great Stoic writer, and said, more or less: look how well I've read it. He expected praise. What he got was a put-down borrowed from the gym. Today: not more books.
screen: `A STACK BY THE BED.` → `TEST ME, I'VE READ IT ALL.` → `NOT THE ANSWER HE WANTED.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter four, on progress. Epictetus answers the student with a picture from the gym. Imagine asking an athlete to show you his shoulders, and he says: look at my weights. Wonderful weights, Epictetus says. I wanted to see what they did to you. The scroll is the weights. Reading it is the lifting. Progress is what changes in you. And he's precise about where to look. Show me your desire and your aversion: do you still want things that aren't in your power, and dread things you can't avoid? Show me how you act: do you choose and refuse with care, or on impulse? Show me how you judge: do you agree to every impression that shows up, or do you check it? That's where progress lives. Not on a shelf. He isn't against books. He respects Chrysippus as a guide. A map is worth having. But a map isn't the trip. You can know the whole route to a city and never leave your chair. Epictetus wants to see someone who used to snap at their brother and doesn't anymore, someone who used to panic at bad news and now takes a breath. That person may have read less than the student with the scroll. They've traveled further. It's a little uncomfortable, because reading is pleasant and safe, and the other kind of progress happens in traffic, at dinner, in the middle of an argument. But that's exactly where Epictetus sends his students, and that's where he'd come looking for them.
screen: `THE ATHLETE'S SHOULDERS, NOT HIS WEIGHTS.` · `LOOK AT DESIRE, ACTION, JUDGMENT.` · `A MAP ISN'T THE TRIP.` · `THE ONE WHO DOESN'T SNAP ANYMORE.` · then, large: `NOT MORE BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and breathe. Pick one reaction you'd like to change: the flash of irritation in traffic, the sinking feeling at an email, the urge to check your phone. Think back a year. Was that reaction stronger then, or the same? Don't grade yourself. Just measure, the way an athlete checks one lift. Then rest with the breath, and let that one reaction be your measure for today. The bell holds the time.
Not more books. Epictetus' test of progress: not how much you've read, but how you now desire, act and judge.
Your line: not more books. Before you reach for the next thing to read today, notice one reaction and ask whether it's changed. Day three hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Stoics keep a short evening review of how they reacted that day, treating reading as preparation and changed reactions as the real measure.

options: asks to see what the reading has changed in him.

original.note: Greek prokopē: progress, moving forward; the title word of Discourses 1.4.

trapdoor: what you thought: read more and you'll get wiser.
what it means: progress is a change in how you want, act and judge.
what a scholar hears: Epictetus' three areas, desire, action and assent, run all through the Discourses, and 1.4 names all three as the place where progress shows.

notes: Discourses 1.4 paraphrased: the student with Chrysippus' treatise (On Impulse), the athlete's shoulders vs. jumping weights (halteres). Confirm details.
'Calls Chrysippus a guide, like a map': 1.4 praises Chrysippus as the one who explains nature; the map image is the script's, not Epictetus'. Check that the voice keeps that clear enough.
Three areas (desire/aversion, impulse/action, assent) are named in 1.4 as the place of progress; confirm.
